---
title: "4. Choosing a model"
description: >
  Five spatial priors, switching the nugget and the trend off, holding a
  parameter at a value, and scoring the alternatives by approximate
  leave-one-out from a single fit each.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
# site builds: GADM files downloaded earlier, if STAREAL_GADM_CACHE names a folder of them
local({
  cache <- Sys.getenv("STAREAL_GADM_CACHE")
  if (nzchar(cache)) {
    dir.create(file.path(tempdir(), "gadm"), showWarnings = FALSE)
    file.copy(list.files(cache, pattern = "^gadm41_", full.names = TRUE), file.path(tempdir(), "gadm"))
  }
})
```

The model of [tutorial 1](crt76t.html) made three choices without
comment: a Leroux prior in space, a linear trend in time, and a nugget for
the scatter between surveys. Each could have been made differently. This
tutorial uses the same crt K76T data to show how to:

- choose another spatial prior;
- switch parts of the model off, or hold a parameter at a value;
- score each fit by how well it predicts the data it was not given, with
  [`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html), and line the fits up with `compare_models()`.

```{r packages}
library(stareal)
```

## 1. The data

As in tutorial 1:

```{r data, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
iso3 <- c("DJI", "ERI", "ETH", "KEN", "SOM", "SSD", "SDN", "UGA")
adm1 <- sf::st_as_sf(geodata::gadm(iso3, level = 1, path = tempdir(), version = "4.1", resolution = 2))
lakes <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(scale = 10, type = "lakes", category = "physical",
                                    returnclass = "sf", destdir = tempdir())
crs <- "+proj=laea +lat_0=8 +lon_0=37 +units=m"
adm1 <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_transform(adm1, crs))
lakes <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_transform(lakes, crs))
lakes <- lakes[as.numeric(sf::st_area(lakes)) > 1e9, ]
water <- sf::st_intersection(sf::st_union(lakes), sf::st_union(adm1))
adm1 <- sf::st_difference(adm1, water)
adm1 <- adm1[adm1$ENGTYPE_1 != "Water body", ]           # what is left of Uganda's lake units
fr <- areal_frame(adm1, id = "GID_1", groups = c(country = "COUNTRY"), link_within = "country",
                  verbose = FALSE)
tf <- time_frame(1989, 2024, "month")
d <- areal_data(igad_crt76t, fr, tf, y = "positive", k = "tested",
                coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), date = "collection_day", verbose = FALSE)
```

## 2. Five spatial priors

At each time step, the field is given a prior on the adjacency graph: how
alike neighbouring units should be. `fit_areal(spatial = )` offers five.
All of them have a scale, `sigma`, and all but two a parameter `rho_s` for
the strength of spatial dependence, with `rho_s = 0` meaning independent
units. In plain words:

- **`"leroux"`**, the default. Each unit is a compromise between its
  neighbours and its own independent value, and `rho_s` sets the balance:
  near 1, neighbours are strongly alike.
- **`"bym2"`**: the field is the sum of a smooth part and an independent
  part. `sigma` is roughly the field's standard deviation in any one unit,
  and `rho_s` is the share of its variance in the smooth part. It is the
  same idea as Leroux, parameterised so that the two numbers are easier to
  read and to give priors to. **`rho_s` does not mean the same as in
  Leroux**, so the two fits' values are not comparable.
- **`"car"`**, the proper CAR. Each unit is drawn towards `rho_s` times the
  mean of its neighbours. Units with fewer neighbours, often on borders and
  coasts, vary more.
- **`"iid"`**: independent units, Leroux with `rho_s` fixed at 0. A unit
  learns nothing from its neighbours, only from its own surveys in nearby
  months. A unit never surveyed gets the regional mean, from the trend,
  and a wide interval.
- **`"icar"`**, the intrinsic CAR: Leroux with `rho_s` fixed at 1, the
  strongest smoothing. **The field then sums to zero over the units at
  every time step.** It can move one region up and another down, but not
  the whole map, so the region's level and its changes over time come from
  the fixed effects alone. Here, that is one straight line on the logit
  scale.

The formulas are on the [Method](method.html#spatial-priors) page. All five
cost the same to fit. With the default settings, each fit takes about as
long as tutorial 1's:

```{r fit-priors, message = FALSE}
fits <- list(
  leroux = fit_areal(d),
  bym2   = fit_areal(d, spatial = "bym2"),
  car    = fit_areal(d, spatial = "car"),
  iid    = fit_areal(d, spatial = "iid"),
  icar   = fit_areal(d, spatial = "icar")
)
sapply(fits, function(f) diagnose(f)$pass)
```

The iid fit fails `diagnose()` at the default length:

```{r iid-check}
subset(summary(fits$iid)$table, select = c(variable, mean, q2.5, q97.5, rhat, ess_bulk))
```

The nugget's effective sample size is low. With independent units, the
field and the nugget are both independent from one unit to the next, and
only the field's memory from month to month tells them apart. As in
[tutorial 2](k13-561h.html), the remedy is a longer run:

```{r iid-long, message = FALSE}
fits$iid <- fit_areal(d, spatial = "iid", control = list(n_iter = 10000, n_burn = 2000))
diagnose(fits$iid)$pass
```

Before any scores, compare what the priors make of the data. The clearest
difference is in the trend:

```{r trends}
coef_of <- function(f, v) unlist(subset(summary(f)$table, variable == v, c(mean, q2.5, q97.5)))
round(t(sapply(fits, coef_of, "trend")), 2)
```

```{r trend-numbers, include = FALSE}
tr <- t(sapply(fits, coef_of, "trend"))
```

Under Leroux and the proper CAR, the trend is uncertain: its interval runs
from about `r round(tr["leroux", "q2.5"], 1)` to
`r round(tr["leroux", "q97.5"], 1)`. Under BYM2, iid and ICAR it is
steeper and much better determined, at about
`r round(tr["icar", "mean"], 1)`. The reason is the field's region-wide
component. With `rho_s` near 1, as here, the Leroux and proper CAR fields
can move the whole region up or down together, and that component bends
the regional curve away from the straight line of the trend. The other
three priors have almost no region-wide component (ICAR has none at all),
so the regional curve is the trend: a straight line on the logit scale,
which the data then pin down. The decline of K76T need not have been a
straight line, so the difference matters. Section 5 asks which the data
prefer.

## 3. Switching parts of the model off

The other parts of the model are switched off in the call:

- **No nugget**: `nugget = FALSE`. Every difference between surveys must
  then be explained by the smooth field.
- **No trend**: `formula = ~ 1`, an intercept only. The field must then
  carry the region-wide decline as well as the local departures from it.
- **A parameter held at a value**: `fixed`, a list of values for any of
  `sigma`, `rho_s`, `rho_t` and `sigma_n`. With `rho_t = 0`, the field has
  no memory from one month to the next: each month's map is independent
  of the last, apart from the trend.

```{r fit-off, message = FALSE}
fits$no_nugget <- fit_areal(d, nugget = FALSE)
fits$no_trend  <- fit_areal(d, formula = ~ 1)
fits$rho_t_0   <- fit_areal(d, fixed = list(rho_t = 0), control = list(n_iter = 10000, n_burn = 2000))
sapply(fits[c("no_nugget", "no_trend", "rho_t_0")], function(f) diagnose(f)$pass)
summary(fits$rho_t_0)
```

A fixed parameter is not sampled, so it is missing from the summary, the
trace plots and `diagnose()`. The `rho_t = 0` fit is given the longer run
from the start. Without memory in time, the field and the nugget are hard
to tell apart, as for the iid prior: only the field's correlation in space
separates them, and the default length is not enough.

## 4. Scoring a fit: `loo()`

`diagnose()` says whether a fit has converged, not whether its model is
good. A model is good if it predicts data it has not seen. Leave-one-out
cross-validation asks that of each observed cell (an area in a month, all
its surveys together): leave the cell out, fit the rest, and score the
cell's surveys against the prediction. Done exactly, that is
`r nrow(d$cells)` refits. [`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html) approximates it from the one fit, in
seconds:

```{r loo}
l <- loo(fits$leroux)
l
```

How to read it:

- **`elpd_loo`** is the expected log predictive density: the sum over the
  cells of the log probability that the model, without the cell, gives to
  its surveys. Higher is better. On its own it means little. It is for
  comparing models fitted to the same data.
- **`p_loo`** is the effective number of parameters. The model has a
  latent value for each of `r nrow(d$cells)` cells and six parameters, but
  the prior ties them together, so the model is about as flexible as one
  with `r round(l$estimates["p_loo", 1])` free parameters.
- **Pareto k** is a check of the approximation in each cell. Above the
  threshold, that cell's estimate is unreliable. A few such cells are
  normal: they are cells unlike the rest, whose own surveys carry most of
  the information about them. Many would call for exact
  cross-validation, with `crossval()`.

The cells' scores are in `l$cells`. The worst-predicted cells are the
surveys that disagree with their neighbours and their own unit's past:

```{r loo-cells}
head(l$cells[order(l$cells$elpd_loo), c("id", "time", "y", "k", "elpd_loo", "pareto_k")])
```

[`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html) integrates each cell's own latent value out before the importance
sampling (the [Method](method.html#leave-one-out-from-one-fit) page has
the details). Plain PSIS-LOO, as in the `loo` package, is unstable for
models like this one. The result is still a `loo` object, so the `loo`
package's tools, such as `loo::loo_compare()`, work on it.

## 5. Comparing models

`compare_models()` puts the fits side by side, best first. It computes
[`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html) for each, and compares them cell by cell:

```{r compare}
cmp <- do.call(compare_models, fits)
cmp[, c("model", "spatial", "nugget", "pass", "elpd_loo", "elpd_diff", "se_diff", "p_loo", "n_k_high")]
```

`elpd_diff` is each model's score minus the best's, and `se_diff` its
standard error. Most of the variation in a cell's score is between cells:
some surveys are hard to predict for any model. Comparing cell by cell
removes it, so `se_diff` is much smaller than the standard error of
either score. A difference of less than about two standard errors is not a
clear preference.

The same as a plot, without the `rho_t = 0` model, which is so far
behind that it would squash the rest:

```{r compare-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
near <- subset(cmp, model != "rho_t_0")
near$model <- factor(near$model, rev(near$model))
ggplot(near, aes(elpd_diff, model, xmin = elpd_diff - 2 * se_diff, xmax = elpd_diff + 2 * se_diff)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  labs(x = "elpd difference from the best model (± 2 standard errors)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r compare-numbers, include = FALSE}
cm <- function(m, v) cmp[[v]][cmp$model == m]
```

Three groups stand out.

- **Leroux, the proper CAR, and Leroux without the trend score the same**,
  within a standard error. These data cannot choose between them. Without
  the trend, the Leroux field carries the regional decline itself, through
  its region-wide component. With it, the field carries less.
- **BYM2, ICAR, iid and the model without a nugget are behind**, by
  `r round(-cm("bym2", "elpd_diff"))` to
  `r round(-cm("iid", "elpd_diff"))`, about two standard errors each. The
  first three are the priors of section 2 whose regional curve is a
  straight line on the logit scale. The data prefer a regional curve that
  can bend. To use one of these priors here, give the mean a flexible
  trend instead, such as the spline of [tutorial 3](covariates.html). The
  model without a nugget must explain every difference between surveys
  with the smooth field: it needs about twice the effective parameters,
  and is still worse.
- **Without memory in time (`rho_t = 0`), the model is far behind**, by
  `r round(-cm("rho_t_0", "elpd_diff"))` (standard error
  `r round(cm("rho_t_0", "se_diff"))`). A unit's prevalence this month is
  a strong guide to the next month's, and this model throws that away.

For these data, the default is among the best. Of the simpler models,
dropping the trend costs nothing, dropping the nugget or the spatial
smoothing costs a little, and dropping the memory in time costs a lot.
Where models tie, the choice is free, and the simpler or the
conventional model is a sound default.

## 6. Checking `loo()` against cross-validation

[`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html) is an approximation. [Tutorial 5](crossval.html) cross-validated
three of these models with ten random folds: 30 refits, shipped with
*stareal*. `compare_models()` adds those scores when given `cv`:

```{r compare-cv}
stored <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "crossval_crt76t.rds", package = "stareal"))
three <- c("leroux", "no_nugget", "no_trend")
cv <- list(leroux = stored$cv$default, no_nugget = stored$cv$no_nugget, no_trend = stored$cv$no_trend)
both <- compare_models(leroux = fits$leroux, no_nugget = fits$no_nugget, no_trend = fits$no_trend,
                       cv = cv, loo = attr(cmp, "loo")[three])
both[, c("model", "elpd_loo", "elpd_diff", "se_diff", "cv_log_score", "cv_diff", "cv_se_diff")]
```

```{r cv-numbers, include = FALSE}
n <- nrow(d$cells)
bn <- function(m, v) both[[v]][both$model == m]
```

The cross-validation columns are means per cell, so multiply by the
`r n` cells to compare them with [`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html)'s totals. The two agree:

- Per cell, [`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html) gives the default model
  `r sprintf("%.2f", bn("leroux", "elpd_loo") / n)`, and ten-fold
  cross-validation `r sprintf("%.2f", bn("leroux", "cv_log_score"))`.
- Both find no difference between the models with and without the
  trend: `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(bn("no_trend", "elpd_diff")))` by [`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html)
  and `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(n * bn("no_trend", "cv_diff")))` by
  cross-validation.
- Both put the model without a nugget behind: by
  `r round(-bn("no_nugget", "elpd_diff"))`, with a standard error of
  `r round(bn("no_nugget", "se_diff"))`, by [`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html), and by
  `r round(-n * bn("no_nugget", "cv_diff"))`, with a standard error of
  `r round(n * bn("no_nugget", "cv_se_diff"))`, by cross-validation.

Ten-fold cross-validation holds out a tenth of the cells at a time, not
one, so the two do not measure quite the same thing. That they agree this
closely is the check. [`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html) took seconds per model, where
cross-validation took ten refits.

## 7. What `loo()` cannot tell you

- **Whether the intervals are calibrated.** A model can score well and
  still be overconfident. Cross-validation's PIT values check that: about
  5% of held-out surveys should fall outside their 95% intervals
  ([tutorial 5](crossval.html)).
- **How well the model extrapolates.** Leaving one cell out keeps its
  neighbours in. A map is most uncertain, and the model's assumptions
  matter most, where there are no surveys at all. Cross-validation with
  whole countries held out tests that.
- **Which model is true.** A better score is better prediction of these
  surveys. Where models tie, their maps can still differ where the data
  are thin, and only the assumptions, not the scores, decide between them
  there.
